text: Two separate VNets can't talk to each other by default, even inside the same subscription — they're isolated from each other exactly as thoroughly as they're isolated from everything else on the internet. VNet peering is the fix: it connects two VNets so their resources reach each other using private IP addresses, routed entirely over Microsoft's own backbone network rather than the public internet, with no VPN gateway and no encryption overhead to configure, and typically lower latency as a result.

Peering always requires two separate peering link objects, one created on each VNet, each one pointing at the other. Until both sides exist and report Connected, the peering isn't actually usable yet. The two VNets' address spaces also can't overlap, for exactly the same reason overlapping subnets get rejected inside a single VNet — Azure simply refuses the peering.

Here's the fact that drives more real network designs than any other single detail: peering does not chain. If VNet A peers with a Hub VNet, and that Hub peers with VNet B, A cannot reach B through the Hub automatically. Each peering relationship only connects the two VNets it directly names — nothing more.

Peering also comes in two flavors. Regional peering connects two VNets in the same Azure region. Global peering connects VNets across different regions, using the exact same command and the exact same non-transitive behavior — it just crosses a region boundary, and has historically carried a higher per-gigabyte cost for the data that flows across it.

The standard fix for non-transitivity is hub-and-spoke: one central hub VNet holds shared services like a firewall, a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, and shared DNS, and every spoke VNet — one per application or team — peers only to that hub, never to other spokes directly. Spoke-to-spoke traffic that genuinely needs to flow gets routed deliberately through the hub's firewall using user-defined routes instead.
